courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
md: Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
md: The context width $h$ (how many previous tokens seed the green list) is a tradeoff. With $h = 1$ an attacker can learn many red lists by querying a detector; brute force needs about $|V|^{1+h}$ queries. But with $h = 5$, one edited token re-randomizes 5 downstream lists, adding about 2.5 red tokens in expectation at $\gamma = 0.5$ (**attack amplification**). The paper suggests $h = 2$ or 3, or its self-hash variant.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: The fixed 0.5 cutoff of contamination="auto" is not calibrated to your data. In the 1000-point evaluation set of lesson 5 it flags 241 points when only 10 are anomalies. Rank by score, or set the threshold from a review budget, rather than trusting the default label.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
md: Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
md: All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
md: Retries nest and multiply. The Anthropic SDK already retries transient failures twice by default with exponential backoff and honors retry-after; OpenAI's guide warns that if you retry yourself, you should disable SDK retries or account for them. Three layers of 3 retries is up to 64 requests for one logical call.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding
md: A 1.58-bit model is not a compressed full-precision model. It is a model whose weights were ternary during training, so nothing is lost when you ship the ternary weights.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: A 2-bit counter can be fooled by alternation. For a branch that goes T, N, T, N, a counter starting at WN bounces between WN and WT and is wrong every single time (100 percent misses in our simulation). From the other start states it gets 50 percent. Agner Fog's manual describes this same worst case.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
md: Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
md: Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query patch outputs to predict the next byte.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
md: Think in **miss rate**, not hit rate. CMU's point: 99% hits is twice as fast as 97% when misses cost 100 cycles, because the misses dominate the time.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch
md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO optimizes for the inputs you profiled. The Clang manual warns that code not exercised in the profile "will be optimized as if it is unimportant". Profiling only a unit-test suite or a single toy input can make the real workload slower.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Assume the model will sometimes be wrong or hijacked, and design so that it does not matter much: isolate the machine, keep secrets and broad network access out of it, require a human for irreversible actions, and check every action before it runs.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: Linearizability is not serializability. Serializability is about transactions over many objects appearing in *some* serial order, with no real-time rule. Linearizability is about single operations on one object, *with* the real-time rule. Their combination is strict serializability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Consistent hashing balances keys. Hot keys need a different tool: copies (replication, client caches) for read-hot keys, splitting for write-hot keys, and miss coalescing for keys that expire under load.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: Solvers do not escape the worst case. Finite-domain CSPs include NP-complete problems such as Boolean satisfiability, so some instances still take exponential time. What solvers do well is prune: most real instances never get near the full $d^n$.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: The state object, not the transcript, is the source of truth for what the user wants right now. The LLM proposes changes to it; code applies them; the query is a pure function of it.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Do not ask about what the state already answers, or about slots marked dontcare. Repeated or redundant questions are the fastest way to make mixed-initiative feel worse than a plain search box.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: CoT monitoring is most trustworthy where the CoT is necessary: behaviors that need long serial reasoning must pass through readable tokens. It is weakest for behaviors a model can do in one forward pass, and it stays useful only as long as training does not teach the CoT to look clean.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A CuTe layout is not limited to row- or column-major, and the index it returns is in elements of whatever it is applied to, not bytes. The same function can index global memory, shared memory, registers, or even map thread ids to coordinates.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Excess loss: measuring how much a domain can still be learned
md: High loss is not the same as high value. A domain can have high loss because it is **unpredictable** (high entropy, like hashes), and no amount of data fixes that. Excess loss subtracts out that irreducible part using a reference model.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: SoA has real costs beyond random access. Adding or removing an element writes to every field array, the code needs one pointer or slice per field, and an element can no longer be passed around as one object. The ISPC performance guide calls hand-written SoA access syntax "messy", which is why tools like ISPC's `soa<8>` and Zig's `MultiArrayList` exist.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
md: The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds
md: Do not drop a deleted node's edges and move on. That was Policy A, and recall decayed over update cycles for every graph tested. Repair the neighborhood (connect in-neighbors to the deleted node's out-neighbors) and prune with alpha > 1.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every offline method, DPO included.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
md: A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss
md: A balance loss is not a free regularizer. Its gradient changes the router toward balance, not toward predicting the next token. The loss-free paper calls these **interference gradients**, and they are the reason a strong $\alpha$ costs model quality.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
md: Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
md: Testing samples behaviors; verification covers all of them. Model checking covers every behavior of a bounded model of the design. Proof covers every behavior of the code, but only for the properties you wrote down.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: Do not copy FP16's overflow handling. FP16 automatic mixed precision skips the update and shrinks the loss scale when an overflow appears. The FP8 paper explains that overflows are much more likely in FP8's narrow range, so skipping would discard too many steps; FP8 recipes **saturate** out-of-range values to the maximum instead.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
md: Stars have no texture, so a plate solver identifies them by the *shape* of small groups. The whole design is: describe shape with numbers that ignore position, rotation and scale; look those numbers up; then verify every proposal against the rest of the image.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Misconception: latitude and longitude are x and y on a flat grid. They are angles on a sphere. Any shortcut that treats them as planar (Euclidean distance on degrees, fixed-size degree boxes) is wrong by a factor of $1/\cos\varphi$ in the east-west direction and breaks at 180 degrees longitude and near the poles.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
md: Tiling turns $k^2$ loads per output into roughly 1 plus halo, and the halo shrinks as the tile gets wider. Separability turns $k^2$ multiply-adds into $2k$ but adds a full intermediate write and read. Large windows want both; small windows on byte data often want tiling alone.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Reusing a freed block on the same stream is safe without synchronization because stream order already serializes the old and new users. Cross-stream reuse needs events: record_stream in PyTorch, event dependencies in cudaMallocAsync pools.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: **Padding by any amount does not work.** The conflict degree is $\gcd(\text{row width}, 32)$. A row width of 33 gives 1, but a width of 34 gives a 2-way conflict and 48 gives 16-way. Pick an odd width.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Low occupancy always costs you latency hiding; high occupancy does not always buy you speed. Use the `launch__occupancy_limit_*` metrics to learn which resource caps you, then decide whether that cap is actually the thing hurting the kernel.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
md: Portable rule for both APIs: never hard-code 32. In CUDA read `warpSize` when it matters; in Metal read `threadExecutionWidth` or `threads_per_simdgroup`. Write correct code that ignores the width, then tune block or threadgroup sizes as multiples of it.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: The split in R1 is telling: verifiable rewards where answers can be checked (math, code, logic), learned reward models only where they cannot, and those kept short because they get hacked.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
md: A common bug is merging realtime messages instead of replacing state. With FULL_DATASET, a trip missing from the newest message must lose its prediction. Merging keeps stale predictions alive for trips that already finished or were dropped by the producer.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
md: Misconception: "the box has 40 GiB free, so it can provide 40 GiB of huge pages." Huge pages need aligned, physically contiguous free runs. After fragmentation, requests can come up short or have to wait for compaction.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
md: The duality does not make Mamba-2 as good at recall as softmax attention. The quadratic form is a way to compute the same layer faster in training; at inference, all past information still has to pass through the fixed state, and there is no softmax to pick one token sharply.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
md: Common misconception: HyDE shows the user the generated passage. It does not. The hypothetical document only becomes a vector; everything returned is a real document from the corpus. Hallucinations can still hurt, but by moving the vector, not by being displayed.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
md: Match the strategy to the budget. Under about 20 trials, use a ranking (a heuristic, a cost model, or a curated list) and measure its top few. From tens to a few hundred, random sampling is a strong and honest baseline. Past a few hundred, evolutionary or local refinement pays off, and a learned model pays off at every budget.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone (pseudo-labeling) is not the same thing. It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
md: Pick epsilon, get a guarantee. The PGM-index fixes the last-mile search to 2 epsilon + 1 slots per level, uses the fewest segments that can meet that bound, and so its space adapts to how regular the data is.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
md: The constraint and the prompt are separate channels. A mask can stop the model from writing an illegal token, but it cannot tell the model what the fields mean. If the model never sees the schema (as with llama.cpp's grammar option), describe the fields in the prompt, or the model is forced through a format it does not understand.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
md: Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Never match binary descriptors with Euclidean (L2) distance on their byte values. A byte of 10000000 and one of 01111111 are 1 apart as numbers but differ in all 8 bits. OpenCV's matching tutorial says to use `cv.NORM_HAMMING` for ORB, BRIEF and BRISK, and `cv.NORM_L2` (the default) for SIFT.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: SISA is a training-time design decision. It cannot be retrofitted onto a model that was already trained on all the data, which is the situation for every existing LLM. That is why the rest of this course is about **approximate** unlearning: editing an existing model so it behaves *as if* it had been retrained, without a guarantee.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: Separate policy from mechanism. Good policies (address-ordered first fit, best fit, segregated fit approximating best fit) gave near-zero fragmentation on real traces once implementation overheads were removed. The remaining job is to implement such a policy fast, which is what size-classed allocators do.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Misconception: "overlapping intervals prove the versions are equal". They show you could not detect a difference at this noise level. A smaller real difference may exist; to find it, reduce noise or take more runs.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: "BF16 train, FP8 serve" is the lowest-friction mode, but it is not a contract: the docs say there is precision drift between the two paths, and on MoE workloads you should pair it with R3 and optionally TIS.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
md: The **good decision ratio** (good evictions divided by all evictions) grades each eviction individually. The LRB authors found it correlates strongly with the final byte miss ratio, so they used it to choose features, model, loss and sizes from one simulation pass instead of hours-long full simulations per design.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
md: MLA moves the cost of attention from memory to compute: one 576-wide row per token per layer, read by every head. That is a big win for decode, where memory traffic dominates, as long as you keep many heads on the GPU that holds the cache and use the non-absorbed form when compute dominates.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
md: Each stage has a different job. The first stage must not lose relevant documents (recall); precision barely matters there, because later stages discard junk. The last stage must put the best documents on top (precision at the top) and only has to be good on a short list.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: MTP reweights training toward decisions that matter for the continuation. It helps most on generative tasks such as code, at larger model sizes, with n tuned to the data; it is not a free win on every benchmark.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
md: SOAP is not cheap in memory. Per $m \times n$ layer it stores $L$, $Q_L$, $R$, $Q_R$, $M$, $V$ plus the gradient: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ numbers, the same as Distributed Shampoo, against $3mn$ for AdamW. For a $4096 \times 4096$ layer that is 117.4M versus 50.3M floats. Variants with a one-sided rotation and Adafactor's factored $V$ cut this to $2\min(m,n)^2 + 2mn$.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: User-space spin locks lack the kernel's guarantee. A user thread cannot disable preemption, so a pure spin lock in an application can always spin against a preempted holder. Prefer the platform mutex, which already spins briefly before sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Snapshot isolation prevents conflicts between writes to the same row. Write skew slips through because the conflicting pair is a read and a write to *different* rows.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
md:
Two alignment bugs cost real F1 and neither one crashes.

Labelling continuation pieces with `I-X` instead of -100 teaches the model that spans can start and continue inside a word, which leaks into the decoder.

Evaluating on pieces instead of words changes the number of gold entities, so your F1 is not comparable to anyone else's. Map back to words first, then score.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
md: aHash compares pixels with the mean, dHash compares neighbors, pHash compares low-frequency DCT coefficients with their median. All three are **global**: they describe the whole frame at fixed positions, which is why resizing and tone changes are cheap to survive and crops, flips and rotations are not.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running the GRPO math example and reading its config
md: The loss config notes that `force_on_policy_ratio` requires `train_global_batch_size == num_prompts_per_step * num_generations_per_prompt`. If you raise `num_generations_per_prompt` without adjusting the batch size, the step no longer trains on exactly one batch of rollouts, which changes how on-policy the update is.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Good NUMA placement does two things at once: it keeps misses local (latency) and it spreads traffic over every memory controller (bandwidth). Losing either one can cost more than the latency penalty alone suggests.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: NMS is not learned and does not look at the image. It only sees boxes and scores. It cannot remove a confident false positive that overlaps nothing (B3), and in dense scenes it removes real objects that happen to overlap.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: Object storage is cheap, durable and shared, which makes compute stateless. The price is high per-request latency and a per-request fee. Everything else follows from batching writes and caching reads to pay that price rarely.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Inside a classic histogram: buckets, cumulative counts, interpolation
md: A classic histogram quantile is an interpolation inside one bucket. Its error is bounded by that bucket's width and nothing else, so a percentile panel is only as good as the boundary you placed next to the value you care about.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: CTC adds a blank symbol and a collapse rule (merge repeats, then drop blanks). That lets a recognizer train from whole-line transcripts with no character positions, and the blank is what makes double letters possible.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
md: `cmake -S . -B build` configures and generates; `cmake --build build` runs the native tool. Settings live in `build/CMakeCache.txt` and persist until you change them, remove them, or use `--fresh`.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
md: Retrying until green is not fixing. The same math that removes noise also removes signal from real intermittent bugs, and concurrency bugs are exactly the ones that fail intermittently. Google's post makes a related point about its own fail three times in a row policy: it reduces false positives but encourages developers to ignore flakiness and delays finding real breakages.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
md: Do not resolve a reviewer's thread you disagreed with and did not change. Collapsing a thread hides it from the list of open conversations, so silently resolving an open disagreement reads as ignoring it. Reply, and resolve only when the thread is truly finished.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: Default to public communication, with two exceptions: security vulnerabilities and serious conduct violations. Each has its own documented private channel; find it before you need it.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: `git commit --fixup=X` then `git rebase -i --autosquash BASE` puts a fix into commit X without editing the todo list by hand. Every commit after X gets a new hash.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Copyleft obligations trigger on conveying: giving someone a copy. AGPL is the exception that also counts remote network use of a modified version.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
md: A small, very stable difference can still be a layout accident: your patch moved code, and alignment changed. If a 1 to 2% win appears in code you did not expect to matter, rebuild with a different layout (the paper calls this setup randomization) or test on another machine before claiming it.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
md: blame only describes lines that exist now. The manual is explicit: the report does "not tell you anything about lines which have been deleted or replaced". If you want to know when a check was removed, blame cannot answer; the next lesson's pickaxe can.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: A fast, exact repro turns history into a binary search: about $\log_2 N$ automated tests to find the commit that introduced the bug, and naming that commit in your report saves the maintainer hours.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Title: what the change does, short enough for one-line views. Body: the problem and its impact, the approach, where to look, what you left out, and links. The description outlives the review: Google notes it may be read by hundreds of people over the years.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: Only **full** blocks are cached. If two prompts share 10 tokens and the block size is 16, nothing is reused. Lookup also always starts from block 0: a shared passage in the middle of two prompts gives no hit, because its KV depends on everything before it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: A wide box does not mean each call is slow. It may be cheap but called very often. The flame graph cannot tell the difference because sampling never sees call counts.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
md: A libpmemobj transaction is about crash atomicity, not isolation. The manual is explicit: "transactions do not provide atomicity with respect to other threads". Changes are visible to other threads immediately, so you still need locks (libpmemobj offers persistent-memory-resident mutexes for this).

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
md: Do not sprinkle streaming stores everywhere. Intel recommends them for memset-style fills larger than about half the last-level cache when the data is not read soon after. On Skylake server it warns that overusing them on smaller blocks evicts lines you need and can hit a per-core limit on non-temporal write bandwidth.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a process owns and what a thread shares
md: A process is a **resource container** (memory, files, handlers); a thread is an **execution stream** (PC, registers, stack). Threads in one process see each other's writes; separate processes do not, unless they set up sharing on purpose.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
md: ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
md: Misconception: rewriting is free accuracy. Besides latency and cost, a rewriter can **drift** from the user's intent (RAG-Fusion's evaluation saw off-topic answers from unrelated generated queries) and it is a new failure point (timeouts, malformed output). Keep the original query as a fallback or as one of the queries, and log every rewrite next to the original so you can audit drift.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
md: A Paxos proposer is not free to pick its value. After phase 1 it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered proposal any acceptor in its majority reports. That single rule is what keeps a chosen value from ever changing.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
md: A citation is a claim, not a proof. The model can attach [3] to a sentence [3] does not support, as it did here. ALCE found even the best models lacked complete citation support about 50% of the time on ELI5, so check citations automatically rather than trusting their presence.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
md: Features used for training must be produced by the same code, against the same index state and at the same moment as the features used for serving. Log the vector at query time; do not reconstruct it later.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
md: The rdma-core man page is explicit: buffers used by a WR may only be reused after the request completes and its completion has been polled. The one exception is `IBV_SEND_INLINE` (SEND and RDMA WRITE only), which copies the payload into the WQE itself, so the buffer is reusable as soon as `ibv_post_send` returns.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Reconciliation does not prevent all corrections. With a single player and a deterministic simulation the replay always matches; with other players acting at the same time the server can legitimately disagree. Games usually smooth the correction over a few frames rather than snapping.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
md: Unhackability is a very strong condition. For rich policy classes, every proxy that is not simply equivalent to the true reward (same ranking of all policies) can be hacked by some policy. Skalse et al. conclude that learned rewards are better treated as aids to policy learning than as specifications to optimize without limit. The practical question becomes how far you can optimize before hacking appears.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
md: Colocation trades memory and switch time for zero idle pools. Disaggregation trades network sync and staleness for overlap and freedom to size each pool. The long tail pushes large reasoning runs toward disaggregated, asynchronous designs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC DeepCAM study, a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: From -ENOMEM and ERR_PTR to Result
md: `to_result` is not a general converter. For a C function that returns a byte count or an index on success, use the raw value: check `< 0` yourself or write a small wrapper that returns `Result<usize>`. Otherwise the success value silently disappears.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
md: A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
md: The Data Buffer is not a separate server process you deploy. It is the data source object that the rollout side uses to fetch prompts and to hold returned groups (for example partially generated samples). With the default object-store transport it is `RolloutDataSourceWithBuffer` (straw transport uses `QueueDataSource`), and `--data-source-path` replaces it.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
md: Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Long-form and streaming ASR are decoding problems layered on a fixed-window model: the window moves by predicted timestamps, unstable text waits for agreement, and silence must be removed or detected before the decoder invents something to say.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Misconception: "out of order is rare, so I can ignore it". In the toy, 5 of 12 readings arrive after a reading with a later event time. Mobile, battery-powered and intermittently connected devices make this the normal case, not an edge case.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: The Transformer's core bet: replace the recurrent chain with attention, so every position can read every other position in one layer and the whole layer runs as parallel matrix multiplications.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: Attention trades sequential steps for quadratic pairwise work. That is a great deal on GPUs for moderate n, and the reason long-context methods all target the n x n score matrix.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples

md: The derivative is not the change in $f$ over a big step. It is a rate at one point. For $x^2$ at 3, a step of $+2$ actually raises $f$ by 16, not $6 \times 2 = 12$, because the slope itself changes along the way. This is exactly why gradient descent takes small steps.

md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program

md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning

md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML as a classifier with high recall on a rare class still producing mostly false alarms. Precision is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$ and depends on the base rate; recall is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$ and does not.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
md: A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search

md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
md: A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and RSS, and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens

md: A visual tokenizer is to images what BPE is to text: a fixed map from raw input to a short sequence of ids from a finite vocabulary. Unlike BPE it is a learned, lossy neural network, so its reconstruction quality caps how good generated images can look.

md: Resolution is the main lever for reading text. Fixed-size models downscale, AnyRes adds tiles up to a grid limit, and dynamic-resolution models spend tokens in proportion to pixels. In every case more legible pixels means more visual tokens.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
md: Tokio's local queue is FIFO, not LIFO: the owner pops from the same end thieves steal from. For servers made of many independent tasks, fairness (no task waits forever behind newer ones) matters more than depth-first order. Locality comes from the LIFO slot instead, which Tokio uses at most 3 times in a row to prevent two tasks from starving the queue by waking each other.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
